finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token with PHP loose equality (==). An attacker can take over any account by sending a token that loosely equals the stored one. Examples: a JSON boolean true, which equals any non-empty string. Or a numeric-looking string such as "0" or "0e0" when the stored token is also numeric-like, for example a "0e..." value, since both sides are then compared as floats. Neither the email nor the new password is checked beyond this comparison, so a successful bypass sets the password for the victim's email. The safe variant reset_password() in the same file uses hash_equals() with a string cast. This shows the intended control, and the loose function is the unsafe copy.
finding.source: Unauthenticated caller-supplied $token and $email arguments, for example from a password-reset HTTP request. If the request body is JSON, $token can be boolean true or an integer. The caller is not in this repo, so reachability depends on whether reset_password_loose is wired to a route.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5-6, an account password overwrite

trace.note: Fetches the stored token for the victim email. The email is escaped with $db->quote, so there is no SQL injection here
$row['token'] == $token uses loose comparison with type juggling, so the check can be bypassed with true or a magic-hash-style string
The password is overwritten for the victim's email and the function returns true

finding.guards_checked: The SQL is built by concatenation, but every value goes through $db->quote(), so I found no injection. The $row existence check means the victim must have a pending reset row. The comparison uses == rather than a type-safe or constant-time check. I found no rate limiting, expiry or single-use enforcement in this file. The strict function reset_password() uses hash_equals((string)) and is not affected.

verdict.guard_found: none (only $db->quote() SQL escaping at reset.php:3,5,6, which does not affect the token comparison; no type declarations, strict_types, expiry, or rate limiting)
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 compares `$row['token'] == $token` with no type declaration or cast, so a boolean true (or a magic-hash numeric string) matches the stored token and reset.php:5-6 overwrites the victim's password. The only caveat is that no caller exists in this repo, so exploitability depends on the function being wired to an unauthenticated route that accepts JSON.

finding.claim: Neither reset function expires the reset token or deletes it after a successful reset. The resets table row is never invalidated, and no created-at or expiry column is checked. A token that is leaked, intercepted or brute-forced can be reused indefinitely to reset the password again. The functions also have no attempt limiting, so online guessing of the token is unbounded.
finding.source: Any holder of a previously issued reset token, or an unauthenticated attacker guessing tokens for a known email. The attacker needs a token that was once valid, or must be able to guess one. Token entropy is determined by code outside this repo.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... at reset.php:15-16, an account password overwrite

trace.note: Token is looked up by email only, with no expiry or used-flag filter
hash_equals check passes for a reused valid token
Returns true with no DELETE or UPDATE of the resets row, so the token stays valid

finding.guards_checked: The comparison is constant-time and type-safe via hash_equals. Values are quoted, so there is no injection. I found no expiry, single-use invalidation or throttling in the file. Callers outside this repo may add them, but I could not verify that.

verdict.guard_found: none (hash_equals at reset.php:14 is only a constant-time comparison; no expiry, single-use deletion, or rate limiting in the repo)
verdict.reason: reset.php:13 selects the token by email only, reset.php:14-16 updates the password on a match, and reset.php:17 returns true without deleting or invalidating the resets row, so the token is reusable; the repo has no expiry column or throttling (the only other reference to `resets` is the same query in the loose variant at reset.php:3).
